questions.stem: The relationship between the internet and the web is that:
options: The web replaced the internet in 1994
The internet is a subset of the web
The web is a subset of the internet — hypertext documents and resources accessed via browsers
questions.explanation: The internet is the global network of connected devices; the web relies on its infrastructure but is only one service running over it (alongside email, FTP, VoIP).

questions.stem: A data packet contains all of the following except:
questions.explanation: It also carries error-checking information. Smaller packets are faster and more reliable — if one is lost, only that packet is resent.

questions.stem: Packets from a single request may arrive out of order because:
options: The browser requests them out of order
Routers may forward packets along different routes to the destination
questions.explanation: This is exactly why each packet carries a packet number — so the receiving device can reassemble them correctly.

questions.stem: DNS is best described as:
options: The system translating human-readable domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: "The phonebook of the internet", operating on port 53.

questions.stem: The TCP three-way handshake is:
questions.explanation: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK — , confirming both sides are ready before any data is sent.

questions.stem: Place these in the correct order for loading a web page:
options: TCP handshake → DNS lookup → HTTP request → reassembly
DNS lookup → HTTP request → TCP handshake → rendering
HTTP request → DNS lookup → TCP handshake → rendering
DNS lookup → TCP handshake → HTTP request/response → packet reassembly
questions.explanation: Resolve the name to an address, establish the connection, exchange the request and response, reassemble the packets, then render.

questions.stem: IPv4 addresses are:
options: 32-bit, written as four decimal numbers 0–255, supporting about 4.3 billion addresses
questions.explanation: The exhaustion of that ~4.3 billion address space is the reason IPv6 exists.

questions.stem: HTTPS operates on which port?
questions.explanation: 443 — HTTP is 80, FTP 21, SFTP/SSH 22, SMTP 25, POP3 110, IMAP 143, DNS 53.

questions.stem: Which protocol sends outgoing email?
questions.explanation: SMTP — (port 25) — send-only. It reads the mail header for the receiver's address, queues the message, then removes it from the outgoing list on delivery.

questions.stem: The key difference between POP3 and IMAP is:
options: POP3 downloads and removes mail to one device; IMAP keeps it synced on the server across devices
POP3 is encrypted; IMAP is not
IMAP sends mail; POP3 receives it
questions.explanation: POP3 = 110, IMAP = 143. IMAP also allows multiple users to access the same mailbox.

questions.stem: Well-known port numbers occupy which range?
questions.explanation: 0–1023 — Registered ports are 1024–49151 and dynamic/private ports 49152–65535.

questions.stem: SFTP differs from FTP because it:
options: Transfers files over an encrypted SSH data stream on port 22
questions.explanation: FTP transmits credentials and data in the clear on port 21 — a direct confidentiality failure on any shared network.

questions.stem: An HTTP 404 status code means:
questions.explanation: Not Found — 200 is OK. Status codes are how a client knows whether to render, retry or report.

questions.stem: GET should never be used for sensitive data because:
options: Parameters appear in the URL, which is bookmarkable, cacheable and logged by proxies and servers
questions.explanation: POST sends data in the request body and is used for submitting forms and creating or modifying records. GET should be safe and idempotent.

questions.stem: A router's role in packet delivery is to:
options: Forward packets between networks toward their destination IP address
questions.explanation: Reassembly happens at the destination device using the packet numbers, not at the router.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: The five Vs of big data are:
questions.explanation: Veracity is the one most often forgotten — the quality, accuracy, integrity and credibility of the data, i.e. the level of trust in it.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Veracity in big data refers to:
options: The quality, accuracy, integrity and credibility of the data
The number of different data formats
questions.explanation: Data may have missing pieces, be inaccurate, or simply fail to provide any valuable insight — all veracity problems.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Big data pushes web architecture toward:
options: Distributed systems, microservices and cloud computing — scaling horizontally
questions.explanation: Named frameworks: Hadoop and Apache Spark for distributed processing.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Metadata in a streaming service is used to:
options: Categorise content, diagnose faults and personalise delivery without processing the full content
questions.explanation: Its three types are structural (HTML tags), descriptive (file names, tags) and administrative (file permissions).

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Adaptive bitrate streaming works by:
options: Compressing the video once before upload
Caching the whole file on the client first
Adjusting video quality in real time to match available bandwidth
questions.explanation: It is a big-data-driven decision, alongside CDN placement and recommendation systems.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: The W3C was founded in:
questions.explanation: 1994 by Tim Berners-Lee — It develops open standards so the web remains interoperable and accessible.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: WCAG is produced by which W3C initiative?
questions.explanation: WAI — WCAG's four principles: content must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. ATAG and UAAG cover authoring tools and user agents.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: Which W3C area covers Unicode, UTF-8 and bidirectional text?
questions.explanation: Internationalisation — non-Latin scripts, right-to-left languages, and localising date formats, currencies and text direction.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: RDF, SPARQL, JSON-LD and Schema.org are W3C standards for:
questions.explanation: RDF represents information as a graph, SPARQL queries RDF, JSON-LD is a lightweight linked-data format, and Schema.org standardises structured data for search engines.

questions.topic: Big data, W3C and web architecture
questions.stem: WebAuthn is a W3C standard for:
options: Passwordless, strong authentication using public key cryptography
questions.explanation: It sits in the W3C's web security work alongside TLS and CSP.

questions.stem: The three client-side technologies and their roles are:
options: Python structure · SQL appearance · CSS behaviour
HTML appearance · CSS structure · JavaScript storage
HTML structure · CSS appearance · JavaScript interactivity
HTML behaviour · JavaScript structure · CSS data
questions.explanation: Semantic HTML elements (nav, main, header) also carry meaning for screen readers, so structure is an accessibility concern too.

questions.stem: Which is a back-end framework?
questions.explanation: Flask — (Python). Others: Django (Python), Express.js (Node.js), Ruby on Rails, Laravel (PHP). Bootstrap and Tailwind are CSS frameworks; jQuery is a JavaScript library.

questions.stem: In Flask, the @app.route decorator:
options: Maps a URL to the function that handles it
questions.explanation: request handles incoming HTTP requests, jsonify returns JSON responses, session manages session data, and the app's secret_key encrypts that session data.

questions.stem: The main structural difference between SQL and NoSQL databases is:
options: SQL uses a fixed schema and favours consistency; NoSQL uses a flexible schema and scales horizontally more easily
questions.explanation: MongoDB and Firebase are NoSQL examples — records in the same collection may have different fields.

questions.stem: An ORM such as SQLAlchemy maps:
options: Tables to classes, rows to objects, and columns to object properties
questions.explanation: Pros: simpler for OOP developers, less repetitive SQL, and it prevents SQL injection by parameterising queries. Cons: overhead on high-performance queries and difficulty with very complex or legacy schemas.

questions.stem: A template engine such as Jinja2:
options: Generates HTML dynamically by combining a template with data
questions.explanation: It is what lets one page template render for thousands of records without duplicating markup.

questions.stem: The correct back-end request flow is:
options: Web server → framework (routing, request parsing, business logic, response generation) → objects/libraries → database → response
questions.explanation: Knowing this sequence lets you say where in the stack a control such as authentication or validation belongs.

questions.stem: A cookie differs from local storage because a cookie:
options: Persists forever and is never sent to the server
Cannot be inspected in dev tools
Is sent to the server with every request, making it the usual carrier of a session ID
questions.explanation: Which is exactly why cookies need HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite attributes. Local storage persists with no expiry and is not sent to the server; session storage clears when the tab closes.

questions.stem: Which dev tools tab shows which files loaded and how long they took?
questions.explanation: Network — Console runs JS and shows errors, Elements inspects the DOM, Sources debugs JS, Performance profiles load speed, Security checks HTTPS, and Application holds cookies and local/session storage.

questions.stem: A browser's rendering engine:
options: Interprets HTML, CSS and JavaScript to display the page — and differs between browsers, which is why cross-browser testing matters
questions.explanation: Vendor prefixes such as -webkit- exist precisely because engines implemented features at different times.

questions.stem: In CSS, a class selector begins with . and an ID selector with #. The key rule about IDs is:
options: They may be used many times per page
They may be used only once per page
questions.explanation: A class applies the same styling to multiple elements across one or many pages; an ID identifies a single unique element.

questions.stem: CSS specificity, from lowest to highest, is:
questions.explanation: element → class → ID — When several rules apply, the most specific wins — which is why over-using IDs makes a stylesheet hard to override and maintain.

questions.stem: The CSS box model, from inside out, is:
questions.explanation: content → padding → border → margin — Padding is inside the border; margin is the space outside it.

questions.stem: Which method of applying CSS is recommended for a multi-page site?
options: An external stylesheet linked from every page
questions.explanation: External — One change updates every page, the file is cacheable, and markup stays clean. Inline is discouraged — unmaintainable and unreusable.

questions.stem: @media (max-width: 768px) is:
options: A media query targeting smaller screens
questions.explanation: Responsive design combines media queries, relative units (rem, %), vendor prefixes where needed, and the viewport meta tag.

questions.stem: The viewport meta tag <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> exists to:
options: Match page width to screen width so the layout scales correctly on small devices
questions.explanation: Without it, mobile browsers assume a desktop-width viewport and zoom out, making a responsive stylesheet appear not to work.

questions.stem: Which is a CSS preprocessor rather than a framework?
questions.explanation: Sass — (with Less) — adding variables, nesting and file splitting. Bootstrap and Tailwind are frameworks; PurgeCSS removes unused CSS; PostCSS minifies and adds prefixes; Stylelint enforces standards; Prettier formats.

questions.stem: The trade-off of using a CSS framework such as Bootstrap is:
options: It cannot be customised at all
Fast, consistent, tested responsive components versus a generic look and a large amount of unused CSS
questions.explanation: The unused-CSS cost is why PurgeCSS exists in the same toolchain.

questions.stem: The difference between a library and a framework is:
options: A framework is code you call; a library imposes structure
Libraries can only be written in JavaScript
A library is code you call; a framework imposes a structure your code fits into
questions.explanation: jQuery is a library (you call it); React and Bootstrap impose structure and conventions.

questions.stem: In Git, git add . performs which action?
options: Stages all changed files into the holding area
questions.explanation: Stage — Then git commit -m "message" creates the snapshot with a hash, timestamp, author and message; git log --oneline shows history, newest first.

questions.stem: A merge conflict occurs when:
options: Two developers commit at the same time
Two branches changed the same lines and Git cannot decide automatically, so a human must resolve it
questions.explanation: It is the practical argument for small, frequent commits and short-lived branches.

questions.stem: Branching in version control allows a developer to:
options: Develop a feature in isolation without affecting the main working version, then merge back once tested
questions.explanation: Version control also provides evidence of process for a project portfolio — a marked criterion in the SEP.

questions.stem: The difference between a local and a remote repository is that a remote repo:
options: Sits on a hosting service such as GitHub, enabling collaboration and backup, synchronised with push and pull
questions.explanation: A local repo holds the full history on your machine — Git is distributed, so both contain the complete history.

questions.stem: Open-source software's most cited security argument is:
options: Community review means many eyes examine the code, though maintenance is variable and support is not guaranteed
It is always more secure than proprietary software
questions.explanation: A balanced answer also names licence obligations that may require you to open your own code, and links to "vulnerable and outdated components".

questions.stem: A CMS such as WordPress offers which trade-off?
options: Complete control at the cost of speed
Fast deployment and easy content management for non-technical users, at the cost of less granular control
questions.explanation: WordPress powers roughly 43% of websites — a useful statistic for prevalence questions. Its plugin ecosystem is also a major source of vulnerable-component risk.

questions.stem: Lazy loading reduces initial page load time by:
options: Delaying the download of off-screen images until the user scrolls near them
questions.explanation: Implemented with loading="lazy" on <img> tags. The mechanism — the initial load fetches only what is visible — is where the mark is.

questions.stem: A CDN reduces load time because:
options: It removes the need for a database
Cached static content sits on servers physically closer to the user, reducing latency
questions.explanation: Latency is largely a function of physical distance and round trips; bandwidth is how much can flow. Compression addresses bandwidth; a CDN and HTTP/2-3 address latency.

questions.stem: Minification improves performance by:
options: Stripping whitespace and comments from CSS/JS to reduce file size
questions.explanation: Tools: UglifyJS, CSSNano. Code splitting complements it by breaking large bundles into smaller pieces.

questions.stem: Adding defer to a <script> tag:
options: Stops the script from blocking page rendering
questions.explanation: Asynchronous loading — async and defer both avoid render-blocking; defer additionally preserves execution order and waits for parsing to complete.

questions.stem: A question asking you to minimise page load times wants:
options: Ways to measure load time using the Network tab
A list of browsers to test
Ways to reduce load time, such as compression, caching, CDN and lazy loading
questions.explanation: 2025 marker feedback specifically penalised answers that described how to investigate load time when asked how to reduce it. Read the verb.

questions.stem: The two technical requirements that make a website a PWA are:
options: A service worker and a web app manifest
questions.explanation: The service worker provides offline capability, background operation and push notifications; the manifest (a JSON file) enables home-screen installation with a name, icons, colours and launch behaviour.

questions.stem: A service worker is best described as:
options: A background script, separate from the page, that intercepts network requests and caches files
questions.explanation: It can be started by the browser when needed — which is what allows push notifications and background sync when the page is closed.

questions.stem: A PWA remains technically a website because:
options: It still requires a browser engine to run it
questions.explanation: That is also its advantage: a single codebase with web distribution, plus installability, offline use, background operation, full-screen presentation and OS integration.

questions.stem: A platform-specific app is distinguished by:
options: Being written in HTML and CSS
Being developed with the vendor's SDK for one OS and distributed through that vendor's app store
questions.explanation: Its benefits — icon access, offline and background operation, immersive UI, OS integration, app store presence — are precisely the gaps a PWA was designed to close.

questions.stem: Progressive enhancement means:
options: Providing a baseline of essential content and functionality to as many users as possible, with the best experience on modern browsers
Building for the newest browser first and ignoring older ones
questions.explanation: PWAs should feature-detect advanced APIs and provide fallbacks — for example telling the user a message could not be sent if Background Sync is unsupported.

questions.stem: The Background Sync API lets a PWA:
options: Ask a service worker to make a network request as soon as connectivity returns
questions.explanation: It is a textbook progressive-enhancement case: valuable where supported, and gracefully degraded with a clear message where it is not.

questions.stem: Which set of measures best describes web accessibility?
options: Sufficient colour contrast, alt text, keyboard navigability, screen-reader compatibility and scalable text
Faster load times and smaller images
questions.explanation: The point that lifts an extended answer: each measure framed as a minority accommodation also improves usability for everyone — clear labels reduce errors for all users, high contrast helps anyone in sunlight.

questions.stem: The standard to name when asked how you would make a web solution accessible is:
questions.explanation: WCAG — content must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.

questions.stem: Usability and accessibility relate in that:
options: Accessible design is generally a usability improvement for all users, not just a minority accommodation
questions.explanation: Usability covers learnability, efficiency, error prevention and recovery, and satisfaction — all of which accessible design supports.

questions.stem: Semantic HTML elements such as <nav>, <main> and <header> matter because:
options: They convey meaning to screen readers and assistive technology, supporting accessibility
questions.explanation: A <div> soup is visually identical and structurally meaningless to a screen-reader user.

questions.stem: Which clause filters rows in a SQL query?
questions.explanation: WHERE — SELECT chooses columns, FROM the table, GROUP BY aggregates, ORDER BY sorts.

questions.stem: SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Country = 'Spain' AND CustomerName LIKE 'G%'; returns customers:
options: In Spain, or whose name starts with G
In Spain whose name starts with G
In Spain whose name ends with G
questions.explanation: AND requires both conditions; LIKE 'G%' matches names beginning with G (the % wildcard matches any following characters).

questions.stem: To list products from most to least expensive you would write:
questions.explanation: ORDER BY defaults to ascending, so DESC is required for highest first.

questions.stem: Which is an aggregate function?
questions.explanation: AVG() — The set is MIN(), MAX(), COUNT(), SUM(), AVG() — typically used with GROUP BY.

questions.stem: SELECT subject, AVG(grade) FROM students GROUP BY subject; returns:
options: The average grade of all students
Every student's grade sorted by subject
One row per subject, showing that subject's average grade
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per distinct subject and the aggregate is computed within each group.

questions.stem: Joining three tables in a WHERE clause requires:
options: Two join conditions connected by AND
questions.explanation: In general, joining n tables requires n − 1 join conditions. Each must be linked with AND.

questions.stem: SQL dot notation (Borrowers.Borrower_ID) is required when:
options: More than one table is involved, to remove ambiguity about which table a column belongs to
questions.explanation: It is also used with aliases and to reference database.table.column. Once a query touches two tables, use it on every field name.

questions.stem: The most common SQL mistake penalised in the 2025 paper was:
options: Missing quotation marks around string values
questions.explanation: WHERE Country = Spain fails; WHERE Country = 'Spain' works. Numbers are unquoted; strings and dates are quoted.

questions.stem: Which statement modifies existing rows?
questions.explanation: UPDATE — Always include a WHERE clause — UPDATE students SET grade = 95 with no WHERE rewrites every row in the table.

questions.stem: SQL is described as a declarative language because:
options: It runs line by line like Python
You state what result you want, not how to compute it
questions.explanation: The database's query planner decides the execution strategy — which is why the same result can be retrieved by very different physical plans.

questions.stem: A PWA stores learner-driver journal entries offline and syncs when online. The component responsible is:
questions.explanation: Service worker — it intercepts requests and serves cached responses when the network is unavailable, and can use Background Sync to send queued entries on reconnection.

questions.stem: A comment field on a PWA renders user HTML directly into the DOM. The vulnerability and its fix are:
options: XSS; sanitise with a library such as DOMPurify before insertion, plus output encoding and CSP
questions.explanation: Verification method worth naming: inject a <script> tag into the field and confirm it is stored and rendered as inert text.

questions.stem: A site loads in 9 seconds on mobile. Which set of changes most directly addresses this?
options: Rewriting the back end in a different language
Compress and lazy-load images, minify and split JS, serve static assets from a CDN, enable caching, load non-critical scripts async
questions.explanation: Give the mechanism for each — fewer bytes over the network, shorter physical distance, no re-download, no render blocking. The mechanism is the mark.

questions.stem: A developer stores a session token in localStorage. The main security concern is:
options: It is sent with every request
It cannot be read by the server
It persists with no expiry and is readable by any JavaScript on the page, so an XSS flaw exposes it
It clears when the tab closes
questions.explanation: An HttpOnly cookie is not reachable from JavaScript, which is why session identifiers generally belong there — with Secure and SameSite set.

questions.stem: Choosing NoSQL over SQL is best justified when:
options: Strong relational integrity across many tables is essential
Complex multi-table joins are the main workload
Records have varying fields, the schema evolves quickly, and horizontal scaling matters more than joins
questions.explanation: Justify by matching the data shape and access pattern to the model, and say why the alternative is worse for this case.

questions.stem: A front-end and back-end team disagree about a response format mid-project. The preventive practice is:
options: Agreeing the data contract — the shape of data the API sends and receives — early
questions.explanation: Clarifying the data contract early is the key benefit of front-end/back-end collaboration, and it lets both sides work in parallel against a stub.

questions.stem: Shell scripting contributes to a web workflow by:
options: Automating repeatable sequences — building, testing, deploying, moving files, running backups
questions.explanation: It is the manual ancestor of a CI/CD pipeline — the same steps, run by hand rather than on every commit.

questions.stem: A site works in Chrome but breaks in Safari. The most likely cause and remedy are:
options: An expired SSL certificate; renew it
Rendering-engine differences in feature support; test cross-browser and use vendor prefixes or feature detection with fallbacks
A missing database index; add one
questions.explanation: Browsers implement standards at different times, which is the reason progressive enhancement and feature detection exist.

questions.stem: An SSL certificate contains all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The private key never leaves the server. The certificate also carries an expiration date — an expired certificate produces the browser warning users are trained to ignore.

questions.stem: For a page that must work on a slow rural connection, the highest-value single change is usually:
options: Reducing total bytes transferred — compressing images and removing unused CSS/JS
questions.explanation: On a bandwidth-constrained link, payload size dominates. On a high-bandwidth but distant link, latency dominates and a CDN matters more — match the fix to the constraint.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest justification for an external stylesheet over inline styles in a 40-page site?
options: External stylesheets load faster than no stylesheet
One change propagates to every page, the file is cached once, and markup stays readable and maintainable
questions.explanation: Maintainability is the argument. Inline styles also win specificity battles, making later overrides painful.

questions.stem: A page uses only colour to indicate which form fields are invalid. The accessibility failure is:
options: Meaning conveyed by colour alone, which excludes colour-blind and screen-reader users
questions.explanation: Add a text message, an icon and a programmatic association between the error and the field so assistive technology announces it.

questions.stem: Which best explains why HTTPS matters for a PWA specifically?
options: Service workers require a secure context, and a worker able to intercept all requests would be catastrophic over an unencrypted connection
questions.explanation: Powerful APIs are gated behind HTTPS precisely because their abuse potential over an interceptable connection is severe.

questions.stem: An INSERT succeeds but the record cannot be found by a later SELECT ... WHERE name = Amelia. The most likely fault is:
options: The string literal is unquoted — it should be 'Amelia'
questions.explanation: Unquoted text is parsed as a column name, not a value, producing either an error or no matches.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly matches protocol to purpose?
options: SMTP sends mail · IMAP syncs mail on the server · DNS resolves names to IPs
SMTP receives mail · IMAP sends mail · DNS transfers files
POP3 sends mail · FTP resolves names · HTTPS transfers files only
DNS sends mail · SMTP resolves names · IMAP transfers files
questions.explanation: SMTP 25 send-only · IMAP 143 sync and keep · POP3 110 download and remove · DNS 53 name resolution.

questions.stem: A team wants to add a feature without destabilising the live site. The correct version-control practice is:
options: Edit files directly on the production server
Create a branch, develop and test in isolation, then merge back after review
Comment out the old code in place
Keep multiple copies of the folder
questions.explanation: Small, frequent commits and short-lived branches also minimise the risk of a painful merge conflict.

questions.stem: A CMS-built site is repeatedly compromised through plugins. The best structural response is:
options: Minimise the plugin footprint, keep everything patched, use maintained plugins only, and monitor — the "vulnerable and outdated components" problem
questions.explanation: The CMS trade-off — ease for non-technical users versus less control — includes inheriting the security posture of every third-party plugin.

questions.stem: In evaluating whether to build a PWA or a platform-specific app for a school project, the strongest justification structure is:
options: State criteria (reach across devices, offline need, budget and team skills, distribution, OS feature access), evaluate both against them, and conclude why the alternative is worse
questions.explanation: For a single-developer school project, the PWA's single codebase and web distribution usually decide it — but say so explicitly rather than assuming it.

questions.stem: Which statement about caching is most accurate?
options: Caching always serves the newest content
Caching trades freshness for speed, so cache policy must match how often the resource actually changes
Caching removes the need for a CDN
questions.explanation: Static assets can be cached aggressively with versioned filenames; dynamic data cannot. Browser caching uses Cache-Control/Expires; server-side caching uses Memcached or Redis.

questions.stem: A form posts a password over HTTP on a public Wi-Fi network. The specific attack enabled is:
questions.explanation: TLS defeats it twice over: encryption stops eavesdropping and the CA-issued certificate stops impersonation.

questions.stem: Which is the best evidence of veracity problems in a dataset feeding a web dashboard?
options: Missing values, inconsistent formats and records that contradict an independent source
questions.explanation: Volume, velocity and variety describe the dataset's shape; veracity describes whether you can trust it.

questions.stem: In the request lifecycle, TLS negotiation occurs:
options: After the TCP handshake and before the HTTP request is sent
questions.explanation: Resolve → connect (TCP) → secure the connection (TLS) → exchange HTTP → reassemble and render.

questions.stem: A dev tools Console error reads Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read property 'value' of null. The most likely cause is:
options: The script ran before the element existed in the DOM — load it with defer or attach on DOMContentLoaded
questions.explanation: null means the element lookup found nothing — usually a timing or selector problem, not a network one.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes bandwidth from latency?
options: Bandwidth is delay; latency is capacity
Bandwidth is how much data can flow per unit time; latency is the delay before transfer begins
questions.explanation: Compression and minification address bandwidth; CDNs, caching, fewer requests and HTTP/2-3 multiplexing address latency.

questions.stem: The strongest concluding judgement in an 8-mark question on a web solution:
options: "Judged against load performance, accessibility and offline reliability, the PWA meets its purpose — sub-2-second first load via lazy loading and a CDN, WCAG AA contrast and keyboard operation, and offline journal entry through the service worker — though push notifications remain unsupported on some browsers, so the design feature-detects and degrades gracefully."
"The site uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript."
questions.explanation: Criteria named, evidence given, limitation acknowledged with the mitigation, judgement made — and tied to the specific solution rather than to PWAs in general.
